Pele Yoetz 12:1: The Land of Israel - "The Land of Israel, the beauty of Israel" (Ketubot 113a). Its virtue is well known, for it is great, as explained in the Holy Zohar (part 3, page 72) and in other holy books - whoever the LORD chooses, He draws near to Him, to behold the pleasantness of the LORD and to visit His Sanctuary. And every person must have his eyes and his heart there all the days, in the manner of the verse (Psalms 42:2), "my soul thirsts for God, for the living God - when shall I come and appear before God?" And so he shall strive with all his might to establish his dwelling in the Land of Israel - only let him first open his eyes so as not to come to regret his former ways and not to need to turn back and leave. And a fence for this is not to go except in old age, after his wife has ceased to have the way of women and no longer bears children, and he shall not bring young children, sons or daughters, with him. And if the LORD has widened his boundary, he may bring a daughter, for she is protected and saved by it, but a son he shall not bring at all, since children multiply and one does not know what a day may bring. And it is true that the air of the Land of Israel makes one wise (Bava Batra 158b), but according to what our eyes see, a person's sustenance is difficult in the Land of Israel, and mostly they are forced to go out, to the point of seizing the mission of a mitzvah to go abroad for some ten years or more, and they and their wives, even more than they, live a life of hardship, and great is the danger of travelers to body and soul, as is known. Not so those who dwell outside the Land, who find their livelihood in their own place. And when an old man and an old woman go, as is fitting, they can live there to a good old age, and even if they live a life of hardship, it shall be counted to them as a good life because of the abundance of good it brings.
Pele Yoetz 12:2: And it is a great mitzvah upon children to strive with all their might and all their soul to give peace of mind to their father and mother by moving them to the Land of Israel, for this honor is greater than thousands of gold and silver. And so shall brother help brother with great strength and might if one brother among the brothers wishes to establish his dwelling in the Land of Israel. How good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwelling together help one another, for his brother is his own flesh, and it is written (Isaiah 58:7), "and do not hide yourself from your own flesh" - and great is such a deed.
Pele Yoetz 12:3: And since many evils follow from being an agent or authorized representative for those going to the Land of Israel - because one must litigate with others in various legal matters over a quarrel not his own, and sometimes he shall need to help topple a man who is already somewhat stumbling, and what does a person need this trouble for - it is true that it is a great mitzvah, but the wise man, his eyes in his head, sees the end of a matter from its beginning, so as not to come to regret his former ways, and every clever person acts with knowledge. And if he can excuse himself in a place where there are others [to do it], how good that is; and if not, let him know what to do and the way he shall walk, and let him stipulate conditions in a manner that he be close to gain and far from loss. And all that has been said on this matter applies to a stranger, but a brother is bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, therefore an obligation falls upon his brother to be of help to him, and it is impossible to say "and be clear of it."
Pele Yoetz 12:4: And it is the duty of one whose boundary the LORD has widened not to refrain from assisting those who go to the Land of Israel, as the good hand of the LORD is upon him, whether at the time of departure or by sending them portions, and it shall be counted as a great mitzvah. And it is true that at first glance it appears that those who go from city to city and burden the communities so that they help them go to the Land of Israel do not do well, and people murmur after them, saying: who asked this of them, to burden others in order to go to the Land of Israel - if they have nothing of their own, let them not go. Behold how many wealthy men, how many rabbis, geniuses of the world, have their honored resting place outside the Land, and behold, this mitzvah is not greater than the mitzvah of the lulav and the like among the 613 mitzvot of the Torah, and nevertheless whoever cannot afford it is not obligated and need not go door to door to fulfill it - for indeed they said (Berachot 6a): if a person intended to perform a mitzvah and was prevented by circumstances beyond his control and did not perform it, Scripture credits him as though he had performed it. And they said (Shabbat 118a): make your Sabbath a weekday rather than become dependent on others.
Pele Yoetz 12:5: And if he is an afflicted man, struck by God and tormented, who has been beset by many evils and troubles, indeed the journey to the Land of Israel is a necessity for him, to ease his distress and as a balm for his affliction - but absent this, it would seem that they do not do well and there is no room to have mercy on them. But since we see that not everyone does so, but only one from a city here or there whose spirit and soul are awakened and who does it - this is a sign to you that it was from the LORD, that Heaven found him worthy. And a person's own feet lead him where he is destined - to the place where he is wanted, there he is led (Sukkah 53a). And it is fitting to help him with all one's might to do the will of our Father in Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 12:6: And the halachic authorities have already written (Yoreh De'ah 251:3) that what they said, that essentially "the poor of your own city take precedence," refers to the poor of the Land of Israel, for they are truly called "the poor of your city" - they dwell there like chickens in their coops, unable to earn a living, and there is hardly anyone found to have mercy on them, and their eyes are turned toward those who dwell outside the Land, both for letters to know of the welfare of their relatives and for portions to sustain their souls and gladden their hearts. And great charity and kindness does one who writes to them and sends them gifts, whether little or much - each man according to the gift of his own hand, according to the blessing the LORD has given him (Deuteronomy 16:17) - it shall be counted as a great mitzvah. And it is good for a man, when he writes to another city, that he write and mention all who are with him from among the residents of that city, for sometimes it happens that through his letter others learn of the welfare of their relatives, and the heart of the wretched shall rejoice, and he shall carry a blessing from the LORD and from men, and his mitzvah stands forever.
Pele Yoetz 12:7: And the essential purpose of going to the Land of Israel is for the repair of the soul, that the spirit return to God who gave it, as it was given, and the soul praise the LORD - for the sanctity of the place and the rest from the disturbances of the age is a great help toward this matter. Behold, therefore, whoever merits to go there shall be holy, shall be abstinent. And even if the LORD has widened his boundary, he shall not indulge his soul in luxury, but rather live a life of hardship and conduct himself in the ways of repentance and in all the ways of piety. And whoever is not expert shall go to a sage and let him teach him, guide him in paths of righteousness, and righteousness shall be the girdle of his loins, and it shall serve him well - he shall bring it out of his body and prepare it for his soul. And he shall be careful with all his strength to fulfill the mitzvot dependent on the Land with all his soul and all his might, for this is the entire fruit of dwelling in the Land of Israel. And the pure man, the master of the book "Charedim," has already gathered at its end all the mitzvot dependent on the Land.
Pele Yoetz 12:8: And it is known that the punishment of one who sins in the Land of Israel is double that of one who sins outside the Land, for it is the palace of the LORD. Therefore every soul-conscious person shall have mercy on his own soul, and night as day shall he cling to it and to its Torah, and shall not be silent, and it shall atone for him for having sinned against his soul (Numbers 6:11) all the days of his life, for it is a time to be gracious to it, and he shall distance himself very far from idleness, but rather shall be holy, increasing greatly the fulfillment of his personal obligation, for it is great. The principle is: every day that they live upon the earth shall truly be for them like Yom Kippur, the fear of Heaven shall hover over them, and great is the power of prayer in that place, the desired land. And they already have awesome prayers that they pray for all the children of the exile, and by their mouths we live. And let each one pray for his relatives according to the eloquence of his tongue, and pray for the building of the Temple, for the ingathering of the exiles, and that God, blessed be His Name, redeem us with a complete redemption speedily in our days, Amen. (And I, the poor one, have already arranged a prayer, and I have appended it to my Beit Tefillati.) And whoever dwells in the Land of Israel must always be joyful in his constant mitzvah, and all sufferings shall be light in his eyes through his love for it.
Pele Yoetz 13:1: Amen - It is known how greatly the Holy Zohar, Parashat Vayelech (page 285), goes to lengths concerning the greatness and magnitude of the reward of one who is a keeper of faith, sitting and waiting for the moment when a blessing shall come to his hand to hear, so that he may answer Amen. Correspondingly is the severity of the punishment for one who does not concern himself with answering Amen. In truth, a man's hair should stand on end at seeing its severity (and I have already copied the language of the Zohar in the pamphlet "Orot Elim" - see there), and hearts ache over the many of the common people who are not careful about this at all. May the good LORD atone for it, for it applies to the whole people through error.
Pele Yoetz 13:2: And since it is written (Proverbs 3:27), "do not withhold good from its owners when it is in your power to do it," how very much must one be careful to say the blessings aloud if there are people whom he knows wish to answer, so as not to withhold good from them - and to him it shall be considered a greater charity than [giving actual] charity, for great is he who enables merit, and whoever causes his fellow to perform a mitzvah, Scripture credits him as though he had performed it (Sanhedrin 99b). And the halachic authorities further wrote (Orach Chaim 167:2) that one who answers Amen should also answer aloud, so that the one reciting the blessing hears him, and the one reciting the blessing shall intend that his hearing the one who answers be considered as though he himself answered, and the one who answers shall intend to discharge the obligation of answering for the one reciting the blessing - and from the one who blesses and the one who answers, praise rises on high, and upon them shall come a blessing of good.
Pele Yoetz 13:3: And it is especially necessary for one who recites Kaddish to be careful to say it precisely - for if he says "yitkadel" and "yitgadesh" and the like, this is blaspheming and reviling [through mispronunciation, giving the words a corrupted meaning] - how can they answer Amen after him? And it is found that besides being punished for blaspheming and reviling on high, he shall also be punished for having caused the nullification of the congregation's response. And one must likewise recite the Kaddish calmly, so as not to cause the nullification of the response of Amen after "may His great Name be blessed" - so that it is found that one sinner destroys much good. And likewise, when reciting the blessings over the Torah scroll and the blessings of the Haftarah, if one says them rushed and clipped, garbled and deficient, he likewise causes the nullification of the congregation's response, and for all this God shall bring one into judgment.
Pele Yoetz 13:4: And over this too the soul of those who fear the LORD grieves, seeing the wrongdoing of the common people who think to bring pleasure to their father and mother and purchase, for full payment, [the right to recite] Kaddishes and Haftarahs - and without doubt, instead of "pleasure" [oneg] they cause "affliction" [nega], God forbid, by mentioning [divine] names in vain, and blaspheming and reviling, and causing the nullification of the congregation's response - and the Kaddish and the Haftarah are disqualified by the resulting flaw. Would that their hearts moved them to give to charity that money which they give for the sake of their parents' and relatives' souls - for even one who has a skilled tongue and recites the Haftarah and its blessings correctly, if his hand is too limited to hold both this and that, and he needs to purchase the [right to recite the] Haftarah at a high price, I say it is certainly better that he give the money to charity for the poor than [spend it] on such favors, and it is more pleasing to the LORD, and more pleasing and fragrant to his father and mother as well - all the more so if he is one of stammering speech, he should not approach to recite Kaddish or Haftarah, for if his father and mother could reveal themselves to him, they would cry out at him and say: who asked this of you? Stop it, for absence is better than the presence of evil. And it is fitting for every person who is concerned about his sons, or some of them, that they may not know how to recite Kaddish and Haftarah correctly, to command them with all his strength that no Kaddish or Haftarah be recited for him, neither within the twelve months nor on the yahrzeit, until they first go to Torah scholars, who shall test whether they know it or teach them, or they hire some Torah scholar to recite Kaddish for the soul of their parent - and this is their honor and the honor of their parent, for as they increase the honor of Heaven, their own honor too shall increase, and they shall merit sons who are masters of Torah.
Pele Yoetz 13:5: But what we said, to recite it calmly so that they may answer Amen after "may His great Name be blessed," can only be maintained when one recites Kaddish alone, but when reciting it with many others it is impossible to be careful of this, since some rush ahead and some lag behind, and the matter is disgraceful. And how good it would be if the cantor of the synagogue, seeing that people recite Kaddish with stammering speech and errors, would himself recite it along with them in clear speech, in order to enable the congregation to fulfill their obligation. And likewise the cantor must be very careful to recite the entire prayer silently and then in repetition, and not follow the custom of some places, reciting the first three blessings immediately aloud and the rest silently - for besides the fact that, according to the mystical secret of these matters, this creates a deficiency in matters that stand at the summit of the world, it also causes the nullification of the congregational response of many people.
Pele Yoetz 13:6: And I have heard from some prayer leaders a reasonable justification: that when there are not many people in the synagogue, they worry lest there not be nine in the synagogue who intend properly for the blessings, and our master wrote in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim 124:4) that in such a case his blessings are close to being in vain. And this is a valid reason when there are few people, or at the Minchah prayer when the evening shadows are lengthening, but it would be better for the prayer leader to say the entire prayer aloud and have the congregation say it word for word with him. And this applies specifically to such a case, when there are few people or it is close to nightfall - but otherwise, for the sake of speed or because of cold and the like, he shall not deceive his own soul by losing much good and diminishing the honor of Heaven, God forbid (and see the Radbaz's old responsa, 94; and more is written on this under the entry "Aniyah" [answering]). And in any case it is better to recite the repetition even with a bare minimum quorum. And see what we have written in the pamphlet "Chesed LaAlafim," 124.
Pele Yoetz 14:1: Brothers - How good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in love and brotherhood, peace and friendship! For if the obligation of love and mutual help in times of trouble is great even between strangers, all the more so between brothers - and let brother help brother. And it is written (Proverbs 17:17): "a brother is born for adversity." And it is written (Isaiah 58:7): "do not hide yourself from your own flesh." And his brother is his own flesh. How very disgraceful a thing it is in the eyes of God and man that there be strife between brothers! Shame is theirs, disgrace is theirs, mockery is theirs. And woe to them if they do not help each other in times of trouble, or if one is wealthy and his brother poor and he does not support him with dignity - for they said in Midrash Rabbah (Avot D'Rabbi Natan, ch. 9) on the verse (Numbers 12:2), "let her not be as one dead" - Aaron said to Moses: Moses, our brother, this leprosy was not given for our sister Miriam's sake, but for our father Amram's sake. Let him take this to heart when his brother is in trouble - let him picture to himself as though his father and mother were standing before him, complaining against him and pleading with him to have mercy on their own offspring. "And whoever troubles his own flesh is cruel" (Proverbs 11:17).
Pele Yoetz 14:2: And in order to have peace between brothers, they must overlook each other's faults and forgive one another and not be exacting with one another, for this is fitting to be the trait of every person, and all the more so between brothers.
Pele Yoetz 14:3: And a great fence to ensure peace between brothers is that brothers not dwell in one house at one table, for wives tend to divide and stir up strife between brothers (and more is written on this under the entry "Machloket" [dispute]). And if they are partners in a store and see quarrelsome words creeping in between them, they shall immediately dissolve the partnership. And likewise, whatever cause brings about division, they shall immediately remove the cause in order to remove the sin. Of this it is said (Psalms 34:15): "seek peace and pursue it." And this is a great principle regarding the ways of peace - to pursue dispute and uproot it at its beginning, before it multiplies and increases, for this kind of strife is like a breach in a dam - once the crack widens, [the whole thing gives way] (Sanhedrin 7a). And further, even when they make peace between themselves, some residual resentment and grudge shall not fail to remain in their hearts. Therefore it is good for a man to look ahead and understand the end of a matter from its beginning, and hasten to find himself an escape with grace and good sense.
Pele Yoetz 14:4: And the essential love is love of the soul, for how could he bear to see the evil that would befall his brother in the world of truth, and the shame and disgrace it would bring to the soul of his father and mother, causing them great pain? Therefore, if he sees his brother walking in an evil way, or doing something improper, or not being careful with himself as he should, let him have mercy on his own soul and on the soul of his father and mother, and rebuke him to his face with open rebuke born of love, with pleasant speech, with grace and a sweet palate and a gentle tongue, and let him say to his brother: let us be strong and strengthen one another to do the will of our Father in Heaven, for such is our obligation and such is fitting for us. And with such good words that come from the heart and enter the heart, let him speak much to him, until he brings him back to the good path. And in whatever way he can bring merit to his brother and his brother's children through Torah and good deeds, so shall he do, and he shall carry a blessing from the LORD and from his father and mother for all the good he does with his brother and his father's household. This is the straight path for brothers, that they not be torn apart. "Let the wise man hear and increase learning" (Proverbs 1:5).
Pele Yoetz 15:1: Unity - Unity is a great pillar for the repair of the world and for sustaining every matter, and the spirit of the Omnipresent finds great favor in this matter, to the point that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said on the verse (Job 23:13), "and He is in one [be'echad]" - it does not say "one" [echad] but "in one" [be'echad], for the Shechinah does not dwell among Israel except when they are in unity. And greater than this they said on the verse (Hosea 4:17), "Ephraim is joined to idols, let him alone" - that even when they worship idols, when they are in unity the attribute of judgment cannot rule over them (Tanchuma Tzav 7). And this was the reason the Holy One, blessed be He, did not bring total destruction upon the generation of the Dispersion as upon the generation of the Flood - because it was in unity. And this, to my mind, is the plain meaning of the verse (Genesis 11:6), "behold, they are one people with one language for them all." And now, since they are in unity, nothing they plan to do shall be beyond them, for the attribute of judgment cannot rule over them. "Come, let us go down and confuse their language there" (ibid. 7), so that they not understand one another's language, so that division enter among them and there be room for the attribute of judgment to rule over them.
Pele Yoetz 15:2: And any group that wishes to accomplish something and have it endure and stand must all be bound together as one, and then all the winds in the world cannot move them from their place. But if this one says one thing and that one says another, and each wants his own word to prevail and not be overridden, saying "ours shall win" - they become separate factions, and "the sword goes forth" and it does not succeed, and they go from evil to evil and come to division, a blazing, flaming fire, and its accompanying evils bring many troubles after it, may the Merciful One save us. And they have already given a parable of a bundle - even one of reeds - that as long as they are bound together, even the mightiest of the mighty cannot break them, but when they are separate, one by one, they are easily broken. And it is written (Hosea 10:2), "their heart is divided; now they shall bear their guilt." Correspondingly, whoever wishes to accomplish something good in his city, so that all who enter his city's gate accept it from him, should not speak to them all together, but call them one by one, and speak to each one with good sense and knowledge, so that they hear and understand and his words enter their ears - and afterward they shall easily become united and all agree with him once they are bound together as one, for if a person wants to break a sack of nuts all together, he cannot break them, but one by one he can break them all. But he should not do this in order that they help him for evil, and should not be like Korach - for one who does so for such a purpose is called an inciter and a seducer - but rather he should do it in the way of truth, to guide them to the straight path, then he may act in this manner, so that they accept it from him.
Pele Yoetz 15:3: And the great fence for maintaining unity is that one fulfill what the Torah said (Exodus 23:2): "incline after the majority." And even if it seems clear to him that they are mistaken and that his own view, which is worth listening to, states a proper matter, he should nullify his own opinion against theirs, and go along with the majority, and not act against the opinion of his fellows - as Rabbi Yose said (Shabbat 118b): I have never acted against the opinion of my fellows; I know of myself that I am not a Kohen, but if my fellows had told me, "go up to the dais [to give the priestly blessing]," I would have gone up. And he also went out to greet those who disagreed with the majority in battle array [i.e., with arguments], and said to them with pleasant speech that it is fitting to listen to them, even though their own opinion does not agree with them. And sometimes the elders and the great must listen to the young and set aside their own will in favor of the will of the young, according to the need of the hour, when they see that a breach is close to opening according to the opinion of the young men, who lack full knowledge.
Pele Yoetz 15:4: And they have already said (Rosh Hashanah 25b): "happy is the generation in which the great listen to the small." All the more so, by an a fortiori argument, should the small themselves listen to the great. And if there is a rabbi, a halachic authority, and the notables and leaders of the city, whom the people have accepted upon themselves that by their word the leadership of the city shall be conducted, it is fitting that no one open his mouth and chirp against them, even if they say of right that it is left. And every clever person shall act with knowledge and stand guard with great strength and might to maintain unity continually, and shall endure and take much trouble, and shall do whatever is in his power to do, for this is the maintenance, the establishment, and the foundation of the structure for every matter and every congregation there is.
Pele Yoetz 16:1: Heretic - A heretic [Apikoros] is among those who have no share in the World to Come (Sanhedrin 90a). And according to how our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained the matter of a heretic, many have stumbled and fallen - may the good LORD atone for it - for they said (ibid. 99b): what is the definition of a heretic? For example, one who says "these rabbis," which is a term of disrespect. Or one who says, "what good have the rabbis ever done for us" - if they read [Scripture], they read for themselves; or one who disgraces a Torah scholar, or disgraces his fellow in the presence of a Torah scholar - and in this especially the stumbling is great. And needless to say if one casts doubt on the words of the Torah or the words of the Sages and mocks even one thing among the words of the Torah or the words of the Sages, this is a complete heretic, and this one throws off the yoke and denies the fundamental principle, and there is no remedy for his wound, for of this it is said (Proverbs 2:19): "none who go to her return." And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Avodah Zarah 17a): this is heresy. Alas for those who are lost! May the LORD, in His mercy, dig a tunnel beneath His throne of glory to bring back in complete repentance all the transgressors of His people Israel, and may not a single soul of Israel be lost, Amen, so may it be His will.
Pele Yoetz 17:1: A Trade - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Kiddushin 82a) that a person is obligated to teach his son a trade, and that he should teach him a clean and easy trade. And it is true that it is fitting for every person to grasp the counsel of Rabbi Nehorai, who said (in the Mishnah there): I set aside all the trades in the world and teach my son nothing but Torah (as I shall write below under the entry "Torah," with the help of Heaven). But in any case, if one comes to set his son up in a shop, even if he is very wealthy in possessions, he should not be ashamed to teach his sons a trade to full proficiency, so that it is available to them, for one does not know what a day may bring, since money moves about - as our eyes see how many wealthy men whose possessions have gone to ruin have been left wandering for bread and asking for charity. But if a trade is available to them, they can turn to their trade and support themselves with dignity. And further, from another angle, a trade is better than commerce, for even though there is not as much wealth to be had from a trade as from commerce, nevertheless one who engages in a trade lives a life of ease, and mostly does not need to travel the roads and cross seas and rivers, nor take the loans called in our language "policies" (vekhzel), which drain a person's own body, nor extend so much credit, nor be struck by his employer and his attendant, but rather does his work within his own house. And even in commerce, a person can choose the lesser evil, and not seek to engage in great and wondrous things, laboring to grow rich through extending credit and loans and traveling roads and seas and rivers, but rather be content with little, and let his business be conducted calmly, with matters close to gain and very far from loss, for "better a dry morsel with tranquility in it" (Proverbs 17:1). And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 114a): eat an onion and sit in the shade [rather than eat goose and sit uneasy]. And the disturbance of the times and the fatigue of travel and the scattering of one's soul in extending credit for one's possessions consume one from soul to flesh, so that he lives a life of hardship and cannot serve his Creator a complete service, but only a deficient and flawed one. Therefore let him choose for himself a clean and easy trade or commerce, and pray to the One to whom wealth and possessions belong, for there is no restraint upon the LORD to save whether by much or by little, and the LORD shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence. And behold, what they said about a "clean" trade - our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Kiddushin 82a) that it should be clean of theft. And it is, because of our sins, that theft has become like something permitted to some masters of trades, such as with wheat, and likewise among merchants there are found several things that are outright theft, only they have changed their name and call them by the name of shrewdness, sharpness, and diligence - but it shall not succeed, as is written in its place. And "he who pursues righteousness and kindness finds life, prosperity, and honor" and shall not come to lack.
Pele Yoetz 18:1: Compilation - How much good the compilers have done for us! Our holy Rabbis, who in every generation merited and gave merit to the many - the merit of the many depends on them, for were it not for them, Torah would have been forgotten from Israel, especially for us, an orphaned generation, orphans of orphans, upon whom the disturbances of the times have grown many, and leisure does not agree with us enough to study with such diligence as the earlier generations, and our understanding is limited. And if we come to study countless books, who could afford to have all the books available to him? But through compilations we can, in small measure, fulfill our obligation.
Pele Yoetz 18:2: And in every generation compilations are needed, as the Rambam did, and the "Tur," and the master "Beit Yosef," and the master "Knesset HaGedolah," and many like them who served as our eyes - and from them let people see and do likewise in every generation. Every Torah scholar whom the LORD has graced with knowledge and many books should strive to benefit the many with matters that are greatly needed, as they said (Berachot 64a): everyone needs the owner of the wheat. And let them make compilations as the good hand of the LORD is upon them - one from summaries of the laws of the Arba'ah Turim, one of principles, one of introductions to sermons, and one of ethical rebuke and the like - whatever they do shall be counted as a great kindness, and there is no kindness greater than this, which is a kindness to the soul, and those who do these things bring merit to the many, and the merit of the many depends on them. And let them not concern themselves with the mockery of the complacent who say: what benefit have these sages brought with their enactment, to change for us what is already known and published in the books - this is nothing but a way to gather money and take a name for having published a book. May their Master forgive those who speak so, for they are not right - for certainly, without doubt, these books of compilations are better for us than all the works of dialectics and sharpness, for what benefit or addition do these compositions give us - most of them gather dust, with none to seek or inquire after them, since every scholar wants to understand things by his own mind and to argue matters of law according to his own comprehension, and if a person wanted to study all the works of dialectics and sharpness, his years would be spent and he would not learn one part in a thousand of what he needs to learn - as they said in the Talmud (Eruvin 48a): if it does not sharpen [my mind], I do not study it. What benefit or addition is it for us to know the debate that took place between two Torah scholars, where this one says one thing and that one says another - and if it is in order to teach the ways of dialectics, sharpness, and keenness of mind, is not the Torah of the earlier generations, of blessed memory, sufficient for us, whose hearts were open like the opening of the Temple hall and whose wisdom is evident from their own words? But these books of compilations, their benefit is manifold, as stated - therefore let every Torah scholar pursue them as one pursues a partridge in the mountains, and let everyone's hand be constantly reaching for them, for in this brief age, brevity is a sharp coin, beloved and cherished by all, and they say, in a manner of elegance (Ruth 2:4), "and he said to the reapers, the LORD be with you."
Pele Yoetz 18:3: And therefore even one who compiles a book of questions and answers, which benefits the many by innovating new rulings and resolving doubtful matters of law, should not go on at length and stray from subject to subject, from the work of answering the question to the work of dialectical argument and debate over the words of the later authorities - demolishing and uprooting, building and planting - saying "this teaching is fine and that one is not fine," for what benefit or addition does this give, and I fear sinning through excessive words. Rather, he shall write brief rulings, the practical law needed for the matter at hand specifically. And likewise, one who wishes to write novel interpretations that the LORD has granted him on Scripture and on the sayings of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, if he wants many to make use of it, should not go on at length and stray from the work of homiletics to the work of dialectics, but rather write brief rulings in the order of Scripture and the Talmud, sweet and pleasant words mixed with words of ethics and fear of the LORD - for the ethical teaching stated on a verse is sweeter than honey and stands as a remembrance between the eyes - and through this his words shall be read, remembered, and recited in the synagogues of Torah scholars and in the study houses, and he shall bring merit to the many, and his soul shall delight in richness while his lips move in the grave (Yevamot 97a). This, in my opinion, is the straight path for authors of compositions.
Pele Yoetz 18:4: However, the masters of compilations who gather summaries of laws must be very careful not to enter into this work unless they can do it properly, so that they not produce an empty vessel - that is, that they have many books, both of the earlier and later authorities, and cast their eyes over all of them with a fine and thorough examination, and not rely on the general summary alone, for there is room for error, and they should not mistakenly record the opposite of what is written in the book, as sometimes happens in these summaries - and therefore it has been assessed that it is not proper to rely on such summaries to rule leniently or to extract money from the party in possession, until one studies the matter thoroughly and sees the law at its root. And I have heard people say that although the master of "Me'am Lo'ez" did great work and brought merit to the many, the spirit of the sages of his generation was not fully at ease with him for having written definitive rulings, for many of the common people, who can read only his book, accept his words as though given at Sinai and do not turn back to ask a sage, relying on him whether to rule leniently or stringently - and sometimes it happens that some law is found for which newer books have since arisen that disagree with his words and rule stringently, and it is proper to be stringent. Therefore one must warn those who read only the vernacular not to rely on vernacular books to rule leniently without consulting a sage, and it is proper for them that the vernacular books arouse them to enter the house of inquiry in order to ask a sage. (And I have it in my heart to write a book of brief compiled laws, but I shall write in it only what is forbidden, and I shall not mention what is permitted, so that no such stumbling result from it.) And it is also fitting for the masters of compilations to do a complete kindness and not simply write, regarding some law, "see such-and-such a book," for it sometimes happens that a person greatly needs that particular law and the very book referred to is not available in his city - and this is like one who is brought to a spring and not allowed to drink water. Therefore, let them also write out what is written in that book, so that the reader find rest in it, since he shall find what his heart desires.
Pele Yoetz 19:1: Guests - The mitzvah of hospitality is a great mitzvah, counted among the matters whose fruits a person enjoys in this world while the principal remains for him in the World to Come (Pe'ah 1:1). Happy is the man who can perform it, having a spacious dwelling - he performs a great kindness, for the value of the kindness grows according to the need of the recipient and his distress and pain. And behold, if a guest comes to the city, a poor man who cannot afford lodging for himself, or for whom it is beneath his dignity to stay at an inn, or there is no inn to be found in the city - what shall that man do if no one takes him into his home, and he is a stranger in a foreign land? To whom shall he turn for help? And if he finds a man who takes him in, he shall truly live. Therefore it is counted as a great mitzvah, and according to the greatness of the mitzvah, so does he give peace of mind to his Maker and receive his reward. Therefore the trouble of the guest shall be light in his eyes, and he shall bear it and not wither. Happy is the man who loves the LORD - according to the abundance of love, no trouble and no money is considered in his eyes against giving peace of mind to his Maker. But they have already said (Chovot HaLevavot, Introduction) that part of proper caution is not to be overly cautious, and it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:16): "do not be overly righteous." Therefore he shall be careful about what is written in the Book of Ben Sira (Yevamot 63b): do not bring everyone into your house - if he knows that this is not a good man, he should not bring him into his house, especially if he has only one room with his wife and household members; if he takes in a guest to sleep in his house with him, it is a transgression in his hands. And even when he takes in a guest, he shall guard his possessions from him so as not to come to suspect him if something is missing, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Derech Eretz Rabbah, ch. 5): treat every person as suspect as a robber, yet honor him as [you would] Rabban Gamliel. And it happened, as told in Avot D'Rabbi Natan, concerning Rabbi Yehoshua, who took in a guest, fed him and gave him drink, and brought him up to the attic to sleep, and removed the ladder from beneath him. At midnight the guest arose and stole everything in the attic, and when he wanted to come down he fell from the attic and broke his leg. Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: the Rabbis have already anticipated you, saying, treat [every person] as suspect as a robber. (And it would be best, if possible, that the wife of the host not go outside in the presence of the guest, especially when she is adorned, for this incites the evil inclination, and perhaps he shall not escape from improper thoughts. But on the other hand, there is a loss when the wife of the host is kept away and does not join her husband at the table, for it may become too burdensome for them to have the guest sit there and they shall not find the right time for him to leave, and the guest too shall be troubled, thinking: how is it that because of me the host's wife is kept from her own house of delights, from eating with her husband? Therefore every clever person shall act with knowledge, and choose the straight path according to what kind of person the guest is, and shall do what is right in his own eyes.)
Pele Yoetz 19:2: And among the conditions of the mitzvah of hospitality is that he receive every person with a pleasant countenance, and it is more valuable and more accepted and pleasing in the eyes of God and man to feed him a dry morsel with a cheerful and kindly face than to feed him fattened birds with an angry face. And if it is hard for him to make a large expense because his hand or his spirit is limited, let him not increase the expense. And let his inclination not persuade him to say that in order to host a guest much preparation is required, as those women say whose eye is stingy toward guests, so that everything in the house seems diminished to them when there is a guest, and they make their husbands increase what they bring by saying, "it is impossible to honor others at one's own expense [i.e. disgrace]" - and thereby they prevent guests and none come. But this is the counsel of the evil inclination, to withhold good from its owner, such a great mitzvah as this. Therefore, if the expense is difficult for him, let him not worry about spending more than what he is accustomed to, so that the guest not become burdensome to him - and this is not a disgrace but an honor, for it is pleasing to the guest that he not increase the expense so as not to be a burden, and whenever he sees that they are increasing the expense he becomes troubled, thinking how much trouble the host has taken for his sake, and worrying that in the end he shall become a burden. But when he sees that the host is not increasing the expense, it is comfortable for him. And with the spirit of his lips he shall satisfy him with good words and revive the hungry soul, in a manner that he eats his bread with joy and drinks his water with a good heart.
Pele Yoetz 19:3: And it is included in this that even if there is anger and distress in his heart for some reason, he shall remove the anger from his heart and show the guest nothing but a smiling face, so that the guest not think that his face is bad on his account. And it is known, the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Bava Batra 9b), that whoever gives charity to a poor man is blessed with six blessings, and whoever also comforts him is blessed with eleven blessings. And he shall never let go from his mind the greatness of the mitzvah and the greatness of its reward, so that it not become burdensome to him, and he shall do it with extra affection. And at the time of his departure, he shall generously provide him with provisions for the road according to the blessing the LORD has given him, and shall accompany him on his way, and through this the LORD shall bless his substance.
Pele Yoetz 19:4: And among the conditions incumbent on the guest is that he not burden the host. And whoever can afford to stay at an inn by himself should not seek to stay in the host's house, and even if they invite him he should not accept until they press him, so that he know for certain that they invite him wholeheartedly and not out of embarrassment - for it is known that whoever accepts benefit from his fellow not wholeheartedly but out of embarrassment has an element of theft in it (Sefer Chasidim, 316). And even when he is forced to stay in the host's house, he should not prolong his stay with him for a long period, for whoever overstays becomes a burden. And if he must remain a long time in the city, he should not settle permanently in the host's house if there is an inn in the city; and if he thought it would be for a short time and the matter has dragged on, let him seek a wise and thoughtful way to move out to the inn or to another house, in a manner that causes no offense or hurt feelings. And even while staying in the host's house, he should not remain in the house the entire day, but rather go out here and there somewhat, so as not to be a burden to anyone. And he should not ask the host prying questions, nor ask him about his business affairs or his possessions. And if his hand can afford it and it is not a slight to the host's honor, he too shall open his hand to make expenditures and buy provisions for the meal, and he shall greatly honor the host and all the members of the household, and show affection and extra warmth to the children, and fill his mouth with the host's praise and bless him with his own blessing. And at the time of his departure, he shall give a gift to the host and his wife. And after his journey he shall also remember them in a letter, and through this he shall be found pleasing in his conduct.
Pele Yoetz 19:5: And upon the charity administrator too falls an obligation to keep his eyes open regarding guests, and according to what kind of person he is, he shall assign him lodging with the residents of the city in rotation, according to his dignity. And for one to whom no host is assigned, and who is given instead a lodging house from the community, as is the custom in many places, they shall prepare the house to be a good dwelling for the winter months, and prepare there pillows and cushions, even if stuffed with straw, and necessary household utensils, even earthenware vessels. And they shall give them their sustenance, sufficient for their need, day by day, with a pleasant countenance. And how good it is for the host to give them at least from Sabbath to Sabbath. And at the time of their departure, he shall give them provisions for the road according to what sort of person he is and according to the community's ability, and shall not be overly stingy, for such a one sins and it is not counted to his credit. Therefore let him conduct his affairs with judgment and satisfy them with good words for the honor of the LORD, for He stands at the right hand of the needy. And their own trouble - that they wander for bread and are wretched and downtrodden - is punishment enough for them, and whoever does good with them does it with God Himself, and whoever has mercy on creatures is shown mercy from Heaven (Shabbat 151b). However, the guest too must not overly burden the community, and should not demand insistently, but rather "the poor man speaks with supplications" (Proverbs 18:23), and in the end he shall be satisfied with what he is given, whether little or much he shall take, and bless the community, and not make strife, and not resort to litigation, God forbid, but rather ask of the One to whom wealth and possessions belong, that He put generosity of heart in their hearts to give to him, or send his payment from elsewhere, for the Omnipresent has many agents and everything is from His hand - grace and honor the LORD shall give, He shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 20:1: Wronging - Monetary wronging [Onaah] in buying and selling carries a prohibition in addition to the prohibition of theft, for one also transgresses "you shall not wrong one another." And it is because of our sins that the laws of wronging have been forgotten by many of the common people, for they do not know what wronging is, but call it by the name of shrewdness and diligence - and this is the cause of the world's continual collapse, and the wheel of poverty turning in the world, as the prophet said (Jeremiah 17:11): "he who makes wealth unjustly shall leave it in the midst of his days." And the word of the LORD in the mouths of His prophets is truth. And if a person is seen to commit injustice and his wealth endures, it is certainly wealth kept for its owner to his own harm, in the manner of the verse (Deuteronomy 7:10), "and repays those who hate Him to their face, to destroy them."
Pele Yoetz 20:2: And this is the general principle of wronging - that it is not permitted to lie and praise one's merchandise for what it is not, or to say that he bought it for such-and-such an amount, or that he already gave so-and-so such-and-such an amount, which is not true. And needless to say it is forbidden to decorate merchandise or mix bad with good so that the good appears to the eye while the blemish remains hidden beneath it, or to show one item and give another. Whoever does such things - "an abomination to the LORD is everyone who does injustice." And needless to say if he commits injustice in measure, weight, or measure of capacity, which is called injustice, hated, detestable, banned, an abomination, and the punishment for [false] measures is more severe than the punishment for forbidden sexual relations (Yevamot 21a) - and certainly it shall not succeed, and his end shall be a base and evil man in this world, besides his punishment reserved for him in the World to Come. It is found that whoever does these things is a fool, laboring in vain, consuming his strength and his days in haste to acquire for himself an evil bargain in Gehinnom.
Pele Yoetz 20:3: And it is known that the first question a person is asked at his judgment is: did you conduct your business affairs in good faith (Shabbat 31a)? And whoever trusts in the LORD and conducts his business affairs in good faith, the kindness of the LORD shall surround him (Psalms 32:10), and the blessing of the LORD makes him rich (Proverbs 10:22). And certainly his bread shall not be lacking, and his sustenance shall be in permitted ways, with ease, contentment, and honor. Happy is he in this world, and it is well with him in the World to Come. And it is true that the desire for money awakens even the clever and teaches leniency for oneself, but of such a case they said (Eruvin 65b): a person is recognized by his pocket - meaning that he should strengthen his intellect and conquer his inclination and be fully content, even if it meant entering into the possibility of dying of hunger, so as not to be wicked before the Omnipresent - such is our obligation and such is fitting for us. And how much more so since, according to clear truth, those who seek the LORD shall not lack any good, and whoever walks in innocence walks securely. And this is a great principle for all matters that a person's soul desires and covets, especially regarding money, which is dear to a person, and the inclination nearby rules and teaches forty-nine pure ways to purify the impure creeping thing. Therefore, whoever fears the LORD shall fulfill "and do not rely on your own understanding" (Proverbs 3:5), and shall go to a sage and let him teach him which is the straight path, and shall not deviate from what they tell him, right or left.
Pele Yoetz 20:4: And there is verbal wronging, which is more severe than monetary wronging - as they said (Bava Metzia 59a): all gates [of prayer] are locked except the gates of wronging [by speech]. And it is punished by the Holy One, blessed be He, Himself, with a severe punishment. And in this too many have stumbled, for they did not know what verbal wronging is. And the general principle is: whatever pains one's fellow with words constitutes verbal wronging. And in order to know by which words his fellow is pained, let him always uphold the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Shabbat 31a): that which is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow.
Pele Yoetz 20:5: And many of the common people have this as their folly - that they pain their fellows in a spirit of jest and levity in order to increase frivolous merriment, and this is like a madman scattering firebrands, and shall surely be punished, in a manner that the joy shall be turned into sorrow. And according to the severity of this matter, one must stand guard very carefully, for a person is prone to be exacting and to feel and be pained even by light conversation spoken to him, while he himself does not feel his fellow's pain, and thinks falsely: what does it matter if I pain him because he treated me improperly - I am justified in paining him; and if it is done in jest, there is no pain here, for such is the way of people, and "I said of laughter, it is praiseworthy." And because of this, no man repents of his own evil, for the sin he committed is not counted to him. But it is fitting to know that it is not permitted to pain [another] with words even toward one who has pained him, unless it is by way of open rebuke born of love - but if he does it to take revenge, he transgresses "you shall not take vengeance" (Leviticus 19:18). And certainly, since the Torah commanded (ibid. 25:17) that a man not wrong his fellow, it did not need to command regarding one's fellow who seeks his good - for are we dealing with fools? Rather, even if he pained him, it is not permitted to repay the one who did evil with evil in kind. And if it is done in jest, it is found that he makes jest with this person's blood, and this falls into the category of scoffing, of which they said (Avodah Zarah 18b) that its beginning is affliction and its end is destruction. Therefore let a person be careful of verbal wronging, and especially of wronging his wife, since her tears are readily available, the punishment for wronging her is close at hand (Bava Metzia 59a), and let him always strive that the spirit of his fellow creatures be at ease with him, and through this the spirit of the Omnipresent shall be at ease with him.
Pele Yoetz 21:1: Duress - The wise man said: every mistaken person finds an excuse for himself on the grounds of duress - "the Merciful One exempts him" - for a person always finds room to exempt himself from any good thing by saying that he is under duress and cannot do it, whether because he prefers to rest, or to engage in business, or because he has some pain, or he is weak, and the like, or because his inclination overpowers him and he cannot conquer his inclination and overcome it. But it is known to all that such a claim of duress is of no avail for the World to Come, and nothing exempts a person except a claim of genuine, complete duress. And in order to discern what constitutes genuine duress and what does not count as duress, let him imagine: if he had found an opportunity to earn a vast fortune, would this same duress have forced him to forgo the earning? If so, it is genuine duress; but if, in order to earn money, he would pay no attention to this "duress" and would push himself, saying, "what can I do, there is pressure here, I must push through" - he should consider what he shall answer on the day of reckoning. Would he not be ashamed and humiliated, having no mouth to answer and no forehead to lift his head, and he shall surely be punished as the Master of Judgment shall decree upon him. Of this it is said (Proverbs 2:4-5): "if you seek it as silver and search for it as for hidden treasures, then you shall understand the fear of the LORD." This is a great principle in the Torah, for its merchandise was light for the Jews [i.e., a wordplay: their business dealings were their guiding light].
Pele Yoetz 22:1: Letter Bet: Blessings - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 35a), regarding one who enjoys this world without a blessing, that his punishment is great. And it is because of our sins that this affliction has spread among many of the common people, who eat and drink without a blessing. Some are due to a lack of knowledge, not knowing that one must bless over something enjoyed; some do not know the manner and formula of the blessing; and some are due to a lack of diligence. And hearts ache at seeing the evil of it, when people go to visit at joyous celebrations, and the house is full, and they are served sweets and drinks and the like, and how many there are who put the sweets and the drink into their mouths without a blessing! And whoever fears the word of the LORD, his heart aches over the transgression, and yet he cannot protest, for he is ashamed to say to him, "why do you eat without a blessing" - and it is because of our sins that we have stumbled into the evil of one who does not protest a matter concerning the honor of His Name, for it is great. And he [the host] already recites the blessing aloud so that all may hear and know that a blessing is required, but they do not take it to heart, as though the mitzvah of blessing had been given only to the wise and the pious. And it is fitting to preach to them, perhaps they shall take it to heart to repent, that they may know that there is nothing in the world from which one derives enjoyment that does not require a blessing: if it is something that grows on a tree, its blessing is "who creates the fruit of the tree"; if it grows in the ground, its blessing is "who creates the fruit of the earth"; and if it is neither from a tree nor from the ground, its blessing is "by whose word all things came to be" - and if one does not know [which blessing to say] and has no one to ask, saying "by whose word all things came to be" over anything discharges the obligation. And for a pleasant fragrance one must also bless, for every kind of fragrance: if it is from something that grows on a tree, "who creates fragrant trees"; if it grows in the ground and its root renews itself every year, "who creates fragrant herbs"; and if it is neither from a tree nor from the ground, "who creates various kinds of spices."
